Separate Contracts 
A party's breach of a contract does not nllow the other party to 
terminate 
a different contract subsisting between the two, or even to 
suspend 
performance of the other contract, 
unless the parties have 
otherwise 
agreed. (But see the doctrine of adequate assurance of 
performance, infra section 6.) "Neither the Uniform Commercial Code nor 
general contract law gives either party to a contrnct the right to refuse 
performance because the other has breached a separate contract between 
them." Northwest Lumber Sales, Inc. v. Continental 
Forest Products, 
Inc., 495 P.2d 744, 749 (Or. 1972). That 
rul 
would have made a 
difference in the foregoing case if the parties th re had entered into one 
contract for "Houston rice" and another for "Lnke Charles rice." The 
authorities 
do not lay down a rule or standard, 
it has been said, for 
"deciding whether a series of transactions 
constitutes one contract or 
two." The cases are not numerous and "have not crystallized an 
identifiable doctrine, though the term 'divisibility' is sometimes used to 
name the issue." Coplay Cement Company, Inc. v. Willis & Paul Group, 
983 F.2d 1435, 1439 (7th Cir. 1993). In that ca e the judges said 
"The simplest and best rule that we can think of is that if the 
transactions 
are 
embodied 
in separate 
documents, each 
complete in itself, in the sense that ascertaining 
the terms does 
not require consulting the document for the other transaction, 
they are separate contracts." 
Id. Does an alternative test come to mind?

for that reason, lose confidence in the performance of a separate contract 
between them. If that should happen, the promise breaker might be 
required to give an assurance of that performance upon demand by th8 
other party, see p. 916 below. If that demand
